{{Short description|A family of simple undirected graphs defined by spectral properties}}

{{About|the graph-theoretic concept|the journalistic paragraph|Nut graph}}In [[graph theory]], a '''nut graph''' is a [[Classification of finite simple groups|finite simple]] [[Graph theory|graph]] with at least two vertices whose [[adjacency matrix]] has a [[Nullity (linear algebra)|nullity]] equal to one and whose kernel is spanned by a vector with no zero entries.<ref name="ScirihaGutman1998">{{cite journal
| last1 = Sciriha | first1 = Irene
| last2 = Gutman | first2 = Ivan
| title = Nut graphs: maximally extending cores
| journal = Utilitas Mathematica
| volume = 54
| pages = 257--272
| year = 1998
}}</ref><ref name="CoolsaetFowlerGoedgebeur2018">{{cite journal
| last1 = Coolsaet | first1 = Kris
| last2 = Fowler | first2 = Patrick W.
| last3 = Goedgebeur | first3 = Jan
| title = Generation and properties of nut graphs
| journal = MATCH Communications in Mathematical and in Computer Chemistry
| volume = 80
| issue = 2
| pages = 423--444
| year = 2018
| url = https://match.pmf.kg.ac.rs/electronic_versions/Match80/n2/match80n2_423-444.pdf
}}</ref> This class of graphs was introduced by [[Irene Sciriha]] and [[Iván Gutman]] in 1998.<ref name="ScirihaGutman1998" /> Nut graphs arise frequently in [[spectral graph theory]] and [[chemical graph theory]].<ref name="ScirihaFarrugia2021">{{cite book
| last1 = Sciriha | first1 = Irene
| last2 = Farrugia | first2 = Alexander
| title = From Nut Graphs to Molecular Structure and Conductivity
| series = Mathematical Chemistry Monographs
| volume = 23
| publisher = University of Kragujevac and Faculty of Science Kragujevac
| location = Kragujevac
| year = 2021
| isbn = 978-86-6009-077-7
| url = https://match.pmf.kg.ac.rs/mcm23.html
}}</ref>

== Definition ==

Let <math>G</math> be a finite simple graph with vertex set <math>V(G)=\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}</math> and adjacency matrix <math>A(G)</math>. The graph <math>G</math> is a nut graph if <math>n\geq 2</math>, <math>\dim\ker A(G)=1</math>, and every nonzero vector <math>x=[x_1,\ldots,x_n]^T</math> satisfying <math>A(G)x=0</math> has <math>x_i\ne 0</math> for every <math>i</math>.<ref name="ScirihaGutman1998" />

The condition <math>\dim\ker A(G)=1</math> is equivalent to saying that <math>0</math> is an [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors#Matrices|eigenvalue]] of <math>A(G)</math> of multiplicity one. A vector with no zero coordinates is called a ''full vector''.<ref name="FowlerEtAl2020">{{cite journal
| last1 = Fowler | first1 = Patrick W.
| last2 = Gauci | first2 = John Baptist
| last3 = Goedgebeur | first3 = Jan
| last4 = Pisanski | first4 = Tomaž
| last5 = Sciriha | first5 = Irene
| title = Existence of regular nut graphs for degree at most 11
| journal = Discussiones Mathematicae Graph Theory
| volume = 40
| pages = 533--557
| year = 2020
| doi = 10.7151/dmgt.2283
| arxiv = 1908.11635
}}</ref> Thus, a nut graph is a graph whose adjacency matrix has a one-dimensional kernel spanned by a full vector.<ref name="CoolsaetFowlerGoedgebeur2018" />

== Examples ==

The smallest nut graphs have seven vertices,<ref name="MathWorld">{{cite web
| last = Weisstein | first = Eric W.
| title = Nut Graph
| publisher = Wolfram Research
| url = https://mathworld.wolfram.com/NutGraph.html
}}</ref> and the three such graphs are called the <em>Sciriha graphs</em>.<ref>{{cite thesis
 |last=McCarthy
 |first=Maxine Maryam
 |title=Topology in finite chiral structures
 |degree=PhD
 |publisher=University of Sheffield
 |date=May 2024
 |url=https://etheses.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/35667/1/Thesis_final.pdf
}}</ref>
Nut graphs exist on every order <math>n\geq 7</math>.<ref name="Sciriha2009">{{cite journal
| last = Sciriha | first = Irene
| title = Maximal core size in singular graphs
| journal = Ars Mathematica Contemporanea
| volume = 2
| issue = 2
| pages = 217--229
| year = 2009
}}</ref>

<div style="text-align: center;">
<gallery widths="200px" heights="200px" style="text-align:center;" caption="The three smallest nut graphs">

File:Sciriha graph S 2.svg|''S''<sub>2</sub>

The <math>n</math>-[[antiprism graph]] is a nut graph when <math>n</math> is not divisible by <math>3</math>.<ref name="MathWorld" /> The [[Frucht graph]] is a cubic polyhedral nut graph.<ref name="ScirihaFowler2007">{{cite journal
| last1 = Sciriha | first1 = Irene
| last2 = Fowler | first2 = Patrick W.
| title = Nonbonding orbitals in fullerenes: nuts and cores in singular polyhedral graphs
| journal = Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
| volume = 47
| issue = 5
| pages = 1763–1775
| year = 2007
}}</ref>

== Properties ==

Every nut graph is connected, non-bipartite, and without [[Vertex (graph theory)#Vertex degree|leaf vertices]].<ref name="ScirihaGutman1998" />
Deletion of any vertex from a nut graph results in a non-singular graph.<ref name="Sciriha2008">{{cite journal
 | last = Sciriha | first = Irene
 | title = Coalesced and embedded nut graphs in singular graphs
 | journal = Ars Mathematica Contemporanea
 | volume = 1
 | pages = 20–31
 | year = 2008
 | doi = 10.26493/1855-3974.20.7cc
}}</ref>

== Constructions ==

Several graph operations are known that produce larger nut graphs from smaller ones.<ref name="ScirihaGutman1998" />

The <em>coalescence</em> of two vertex-rooted graphs <math>(G_1,v_1)</math> and <math>(G_2,v_2)</math> is obtained from the disjoint union of <math>G_1</math> and <math>G_2</math> by identifying <math>v_1</math> and <math>v_2</math> as a single vertex. If <math>G_1</math> and <math>G_2</math> are nut graphs, then their coalescence at arbitrary chosen vertices is again a nut graph.<ref name="Sciriha2008" />

== Recognition and generation ==

Nut graphs can be recognized by determining the [[Rank (linear algebra)|rank]] or [[Nullity (graph theory)|nullity]] of the adjacency matrix and checking whether a vector spanning the nullspace has a zero coordinate.<ref name="CoolsaetFowlerGoedgebeur2018" />

<em>Nutgen</em> is a generator for nut graphs.<ref name="Nutgen">{{cite web
 | title = Nutgen
 | publisher = Combinatorial algorithms and algorithmic graph theory, Ghent University
 | url = https://caagt.ugent.be/nutgen/
}}</ref>
Nutgen has been used to generate all non-isomorphic nut graphs up to 13 vertices and all chemical nut graphs up to 22 vertices.{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}} Further enumerations include nut graphs among [[Cubic graph|cubic]] [[Polyhedral graph|polyhedral graphs]] up to 34 vertices, nut graphs among [[Fullerene|fullerene graphs]] up to 250 vertices, and regular nut graphs for degrees up to 8. Catalogues of these nut graphs are available in the House of Graphs.<ref>{{cite web
 | title = Nut graphs
 | website = House of Graphs
 | url = https://houseofgraphs.org/meta-directory/nut
}}</ref>
The generation of nut graphs up to [[Graph isomorphism|isomorphism]] can be performed by an algorithm based on the canonical construction path method.<ref name="CoolsaetFowlerGoedgebeur2018" />

| journal = MATCH Communications in Mathematical and in Computer Chemistry

== Generalisations ==

The notion of a nut graph has been extended to [[signed graph|signed graphs]].<ref name="BasicFowlerPisanskiSciriha2022">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Bašić | first1 = Nino
 | last2 = Fowler | first2 = Patrick W.
 | last3 = Pisanski | first3 = Tomaž
 | last4 = Sciriha | first4 = Irene
 | title = On singular signed graphs with nullspace spanned by a full vector: signed nut graphs
 | journal = Discussiones Mathematicae Graph Theory
 | volume = 42
 | issue = 4
 | pages = 1351--1382
 | year = 2022
}}</ref>

There are directed analogues of nut graphs. For a [[directed graph]], the adjacency matrix need not be symmetric, so the right kernel and left kernel may differ. A digraph whose right kernel is spanned by a full vector is called <em>dextro-nut</em>, and a digraph whose left kernel is spanned by a full vector is called <em>laevo-nut</em>. A digraph satisfying both conditions is called <em>bi-nut</em>. A digraph is <em>ambi-nut</em> if it is bi-nut and its kernel and co-kernel are spanned by the same full vector.<ref name="BasicFowlerMcCarthyPotocnik2026">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Bašić | first1 = Nino
 | last2 = Fowler | first2 = Patrick W.
 | last3 = McCarthy | first3 = Maxine M.
 | last4 = Potočnik | first4 = Primož
 | title = Nut digraphs
 | journal = Discrete Applied Mathematics
 | volume = 383
 | pages = 203--226
 | year = 2026
}}</ref>
